beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new; a section heading

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output. You need a check.
beats.got: Reading the output won't tell me whether the agent is safe, so I need a repeatable check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new; a list of reading I probably haven't done

beats.trigger: **Distinguish** compliant, violating and "I can't tell" for each rule
beats.got: A third verdict besides pass and fail is useful to me. The rest of the list is jargon for now.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I should decide what I'd check before the pricing working group sees anything.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent's text becomes real actions through tools, so a vague tool or misleading context carries into the action. It's a bit abstract, but it explains why this module exists.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: I wouldn't bet my job on my pricing agent being safe, and I haven't checked.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: nothing new; I know old security assumed predictable software

beats.trigger: The attack surface is the instruction set.
beats.got: A document the agent reads can talk it into doing harm, so ordinary text is the attack surface. That matters because my agents read lots of vendor and churn material.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: There are five concrete mitigations I can pick from. Gate and scope map to things I already do with people.

beats.trigger: *the residual risk is X; if Y happens, we made it less likely, not prevented it.*
beats.got: I write down the risk that's left and sign for it, which is how my CFO already thinks about risk.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: After adding context to the agents, the next move is to restrict what they can reach.

beats.trigger: Every door you don't open is a residual risk you don't have to name, mitigate or re-test.
beats.got: This is mostly the previous slide again. The customer-language example is the one new thing.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new; it repeats that the loop matters more than certainty

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: A skill is a saved, rerunnable check. That's different from a clever prompt, and it's what I'd want my team to have.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The raw run shows which policy rules the agent can check against my system and which it can't.

beats.trigger: the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript.
beats.got: I tell the agent which data and customers matter to us, so the check isn't generic. That's the part only I know.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: The agent will interview me for a while before it writes the check. The wait is acceptable if the output is reusable.

beats.trigger: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."
beats.got: I answer what I know and hand the rest back to the agent, then check its list for the named risk patterns and make the rules sound like us.

beats.trigger: The skill loads in your next session in this training directory.
beats.got: The skill gets saved as files in my own directory. Nothing here shows how a colleague would get it.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: nothing new beyond the point that agent mitigations add to our existing controls and don't replace them

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: I'm not after a pass. I run the check, fix one thing and record what's left.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Typing / shows whether my skill is available, which is a quick sanity check.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: My own check can surface things I missed and show that some things I considered settled aren't. That's the contradiction-finding I value.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The unease I get reading the ranked risk report is the signal to act on.

beats.trigger: Pick one risk from the two reports: the one that bugs you on the second skim.
beats.got: I choose the risk that bothers me most, the agent applies a mitigation, and I re-run and read what remains.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: For hard calls I take the report and one narrow question to legal or security. That's workable for me.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: We fixed one risk, so my pricing agent is still a prototype until I do the rest.

beats.trigger: Certainty is not on offer. The discipline is the loop: assess, mitigate, reassess the residual, decide.
beats.got: nothing new; the lecture's loop again, plus the name Recipe 4

beats.trigger: Two things travel: the reusable check, and the root instructions file's rules for the risk you found.
beats.got: The agent adds rules to the root instructions file, so the next session starts knowing what I found, and I can correct those rules.

beats.trigger: To share, give a teammate the skill and install it in their runtime.
beats.got: A skill can be handed to a colleague. It's still copies per person, which is the problem my team already has, but I'm told Module 7 covers sharing.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer.
beats.got: nothing new; a recap

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: There's homework before Module 5. I'd probably skim it, and the 'your call' line reads slightly pushy.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two public cases of AI output going out unchecked; I'm to find the missing check.

take_homes: Reading the output won't tell me if an agent is safe. I need a rerunnable check, and I now have a saved skill that runs one on my system.
Text the agent reads can steer it, so scoping what it can reach beats hoping it behaves. Scope, split, filter, gate and review are my options.
Write down the residual risk and sign for it. 'I can't tell' is an acceptable answer, and I take the report to legal or security when it's too hard for me.

monday.move: Run the agent-audit skill on the usage-pricing pilot-cohort brief setup. Pick the one risk that bothers me and apply one mitigation, probably scoping the sources it reads or a human gate before it goes to the working group. Write the residual into the report.
monday.who: Me first. Then I show the report to the pricing working group and ask legal one narrow question.
monday.when: Monday morning, before the working group brief goes out
monday.stop_condition: One risk mitigated, one residual written down and accepted, and the 'I can't tell' rows listed for legal
monday.blocker: The skill lives only in my directory and my team has no shared place for it, so my fourteen people can't run it.

misconception.why: I came in thinking 'good at this' meant better prompts. A saved check that carries the judgment, reruns, and finds things I hadn't thought of is clearly worth more than a better prompt. I still think prompt quality matters for the other modules, so it isn't fully changed.

one_line: Useful, because I built a check I can rerun on the pricing agent, but the lecture repeats itself and nothing says how my team shares the check.
